Creation, retention and exit, replicated

The whole database was rebuilt from scratch by new agents that never saw the original data, code or results. They re-ran the 24-sector search in every country, re-downloaded every covariate, and re-ran every model from a written spec. The core finding replicates: independent platform firms rise and then fall with state capacity, because acquisition, not failure, absorbs them at the top. The finer claims about which part of the state drives it do not. The fiscal-capacity story in panels 12–13 is the main casualty.

4,768 firms · 212 searched countries (165 with a Hanson–Sigman score) · negative binomial, Lind–Mehlum test · original: 1,883 firms, 162 countries

Tally: of 36 claims, 20 replicate, 5 replicate partly and 11 do not. Everything about the shape of the relationship and the acquisition mechanism holds, and several results are sharper on the larger sample. What fails is the attempt in panels 09 and 12–13 to pin the hump on the fiscal dimension. In the new data, rule of law, judicial checks and plain development all bend too once the same controls go in, so the evidence no longer singles out fiscal capacity.

Blindness. Every step after writing the protocol was done by an agent with no previous context. None of them could see the original data, the original numbers, your analogues site or this page, and each was told not to look for them. The search protocol and the analysis spec describe the method only: the definition of an analogue, the 24-sector checklist, the outcome coding, the Lind–Mehlum test and the list of panels. One gap remains. The analysis agent's working folder also held a file of the original page's data. The agent reported it did not open it, and nothing in its output suggests otherwise.

Differences in the data build.
• Passes: one depth pass per region (20 agents; 15 were cut off by a usage limit and finished by continuation agents), rather than a shallow pass followed by a depth pass.
• Size: 4,826 raw entries, 4,771 after 44 duplicates and 11 US-territory firms were removed, and 4,768 after the verification pass below.
• Repair pass: a second pass by 19 agents made 1,960 repairs, 1,930 of them filling missing founding years, outcomes and exit years. 204 outcomes remain unknown. The headline test is unchanged whether they are coded independent or shut down (p = 0.0012 either way).
• Zero countries: only 5 of the 165 scored countries have zero firms, against 16 of 162 originally. Pushing hard on small markets turned up at least one qualifying firm almost everywhere.
• No facts from memory: every fact an agent had filled in from its own knowledge (574 facts across 480 firms) was looked up again by eight verification agents. 415 were confirmed with a fetched source, 38 were corrected to the sourced value, and 121 could not be sourced and were blanked. Three firms whose country of origin rested only on memory were dropped. The 18 memory-based founding years for US analogues were also checked: 17 were confirmed, and the one that could not be sourced was already blank.

What the larger sample changes. The replication finds 2.5 times as many firms, including many more small firms and domestic roll-ups. That shifts the acquirer mix toward domestic buyers (panel 07), moves the peak somewhat left (1.19 against 1.45, with overlapping intervals), and makes the Medium–High difference in panel 06 detectable.

Covariates. The versions differ from the original's. Hanson–Sigman v1 comes via OWID as before, V-Dem v16 via OWID, and GRD 2025 comes directly from UNU-WIDER (the original used the 2022 release). GRD values are general government where available. The original is a merged general/central file, which is one plausible source of the fiscal differences. All development covariates are 2015 World Bank or UNDP values.

Statistics. The survival and sandwich packages installed this time. The log-rank tests and clustered standard errors on this page therefore come from survival::survdiff and sandwich::vcovCL, not the hand-rolled versions the original had to use.

01

Every country in the data

One dot per country. Height is how many platform firms it has; colour is how many of those are still independent.

Mostly acquired / exited Mostly independent No firms found (5 countries)

Hover a dot for that country's numbers, or click it to open its full profile and firm list. The same drift as the original: small, independence-heavy markets on the left and larger, more-acquired markets on the right.

India and China still dominate the raw counts (324 and 181 firms), followed by Germany (134), Brazil (132) and Nigeria (127). Only 5 scored countries came up empty: Burundi, Eritrea, Equatorial Guinea, Lesotho and the Solomon Islands. The original had 16. A further 35 searched countries with 188 firms have no Hanson–Sigman score and drop out of every country-level model, as they did originally.

Every firm, by what happened to it

What happened to firms across the whole capacity range, as a share of the firms at each point.

Independent: never exited Acquired, listed, or merged: still operating Shut down

Read the bands top to bottom at any capacity level; they always sum to 100%. The orange band shrinks from left to right, as in the original.

Hover a country’s dot for its exact split across outcomes. Click it to open the full profile, or click a legend label to isolate one band.

4,398 firms have both a capacity score and a known outcome: 2,723 independent, 1,277 acquired, listed, merged or delisted, and 398 shut down. The shutdown band is slightly thicker at the far left than in the original. That fits panel 04: in the replication, shutdown does not rise with capacity at all.

03

The same data, two definitions of survival

Fitted firm counts against state capacity, under two different definitions of a firm having survived.

Still operating: everything but shutdowns Never exited: independent firms only

Orange counts only firms that never exited; blue counts everything except shutdowns. Orange rises then falls; blue keeps climbing. Faded dots are the raw country counts the curves are fitted to.

The same picture as the original, with the peak a little further left. The independent-only curve peaks at capacity 1.19, with a Fieller 95% interval of 0.89 to 1.79, and 36 of 165 countries lie beyond it. The original peak was 1.45 [1.15, 2.05], so the intervals overlap substantially. At 1.19 the peak sits at the level of Bulgaria (1.17) and Oman (1.20), a tier below Chile and Hungary. The still-operating curve's turning point, 1.88, sits near the top of the data, where only 15 countries lie beyond it.

04

What actually happens to the firms

The same outcomes as shares, grouped into six bands of state capacity.

Independent Listed (IPO) Acquired Shut down Merged / delisted

Each bar sums to 100%. Follow the orange band (independent) shrinking left to right and the blue band (acquired) taking its place. Click any band for the firms founded in that capacity range.

Independence falls from 83% to 38% and acquisition rises from 3% to 38%. This is almost exactly the original's 84→37% and 5→30%. One band is non-monotone: 0.3–0.8, where India's 324 and China's 181 firms sit and the IPO share is unusually high.

The shutdown result differs from the original. Shutdown runs 6–14% and has no relationship with capacity. The clustered logit coefficient is 0.03 (p = 0.83) raw and −0.05 (p = 0.69) with firm age controlled. The original found a weak positive age-adjusted effect. Here the substitution is purely independence into acquisition.

Age confounds acquisition exactly as before. The median founding year is 2018 in Low countries and 2013 in High (originally 2017 and 2011). Controlling for age shrinks the acquisition coefficient from 0.79 to 0.53, 33% against the original's 30%, and it stays at p ≈ 10⁻¹². In the age-matched 2010–18 subsample, acquisition runs 9.7% / 13.9% / 25.4% across Low / Medium / High, against the original's 10.3% to 25.3%.

05

The formal test

Whether the downturn at high capacity is real, or just the shape a quadratic always draws.

DefinitionTurning pointSlope at x minSlope at x maxpVerdict

Each row needs both ends to clear zero: clearly rising at the left, clearly falling at the right. Only the independent-only measure manages it, as in the original.

How to read this table. Each row is its own test of whether the downturn at the high end is real.
Independent onlyp = 0.0012. The slope at maximum capacity is −0.93 (se 0.31), clearly below zero.
Still operatingp = 0.099. The slope at maximum capacity is −0.41 (se 0.32), which cannot be told apart from flat. Read it as saturating, as the original did.

Robustness, all on the independent curve.
• Dropping China and India: p = 0.0033 (original 0.020).
• Controlling for log population and log GDP per capita: p = 1.7×10⁻⁶ (original 0.013). The peak moves to 0.69.
• Population offset (firms per capita): p = 0.024.
• Unknown outcomes: coding the 182 unknown-outcome firms as independent gives p = 0.0012.
Every check the original ran still passes, and most pass more comfortably.

Same age, different odds

The cumulative chance of being acquired, plotted against a firm's age rather than the calendar year.

Compare the curves at the same point on the x-axis, which means firms of the same age. High-capacity firms sit above low-capacity ones at every age.

By year 15, 15.3% of Low-tercile firms have been bought, against 26.1% in Medium and 33.0% in High. This is almost identical to the original's 14.9 / 26.4 / 31.1%. The terciles are empirical terciles of firm-level Hanson–Sigman scores, cut at 0.66 and 1.02, with n = 1,388 / 1,238 / 1,298. 474 firms were dropped for a missing founding or acquisition year.

07

Who acquires whom

Where the buyers are. Every acquisition with a recorded acquirer, with ribbon width showing the number of firms.

Left is where the firm was founded, right is where its buyer sits. Hover any ribbon for the firm count and the disclosed deal value.

Just over half of acquisitions go abroad, not two thirds. Of 885 acquisitions with a known buyer country, 465 (53%) went to a foreign buyer and 420 (47%) stayed domestic. The original had 66% foreign. The larger search found many more small domestic roll-ups, led by India (60), China, Russia and Brazil (31 each), Germany (25) and Korea (21). The United States is still the largest single foreign buyer, with 127 firms (27% of foreign deals), followed by Germany (46) and the UK (30). Disclosed value is still lopsided: $112.7bn foreign against $17.6bn domestic across 170 priced deals. The same megadeals lead the list: Afterpay→Block $29bn and Flipkart→Walmart $16bn.

Acquirer country here is the ultimate parent at the time of the deal. That rule was written into the search protocol. The original took the first country named in a free-text field.

08

Does state capacity decide whether the money stays home?

The share of each capacity tercile's acquisitions that went to a buyer in the same country.

If stronger states kept more wealth at home, the green band would grow steadily left to right. It peaks in the middle again, but less sharply than in the original.

Medium-capacity countries still keep the most, but the gap to High has narrowed. Domestic buyers take 56% of acquisitions in Medium countries (125 of 225; 95% interval 49–62%). High countries now sit at 46% (281 of 611; 42–50%), against the original's 28%. Low is 29% (12 of 42; 17–44%). The middle peak survives, though the Medium and High intervals now overlap slightly. High-capacity markets keep far more at home than the original suggested: most of the money still leaves strong states, but the margin is small (54% against the original’s 72%).

09

Which piece of state capacity is doing the work?

The same curve test, run against seven different measures of governance and capacity.

Orange means the test rejects and there is a real hump; grey means it does not. All seven panels share one axis and one scale, so the shapes are directly comparable.

Two of seven bend again, but not the same two. The composite bends (p = 0.0012), and so does rule of law (p = 0.0033), which failed in the original (0.24). Tax revenue, which passed in the original (0.027), now fails badly (p = 0.46). Judicial checks (0.10) and corruption (0.08) are close to the line, and administration (0.23) and civil society (0.29) are not. The original's conclusion that the hump is fiscal rather than legal is not supported here. If anything, the ranking runs the other way.

Why this can flip between samples. The seven measures are highly collinear: pairwise correlations run from 0.38 to 0.92, with rule of law against corruption at −0.92 and rule of law against judicial checks at 0.91. Which one crosses p = 0.05 in a bivariate test is fragile, so a small change in which countries have firms can move it.

10

The same seven, against what happens to the firms

Firm outcomes by tercile of each of those same seven measures.

Each bar sums to 100%. The grey subtitle over each panel gives the acquisition rate from bottom to top tercile.

As in the original, almost everything works here. Acquisition roughly doubles or triples from the bottom to the top tercile of every measure, and runs in reverse for corruption, which is scored so that higher means worse. As before, this is one finding seen seven times: the composition result is robust, but it says little about mechanism.

How hard each result actually is

The seven curve tests put through three progressively harder robustness checks.

MeasureOwn sampleCommon sampleDrop CHN+INDAICPseudo-R²

Orange p-values clear the 0.05 bar; grey ones do not. Read across a row to see which checks that measure survives.

The composite survives every check, as it did originally. On the common 139-country sample p = 0.0017, and with China and India dropped p = 0.0033. Rule of law survives the leverage check (0.019) but not the common sample (0.060). Tax survives nothing. The composite again fits best: its pseudo-R² is 0.023, against 0.007 for rule of law and under 0.004 for everything else.

The tax measure's missingness is again not random.
26 countries droppedThese include Russia, Nigeria, Egypt, Vietnam, Iraq, Libya, Qatar, Oman, Ethiopia, the DPRK and Taiwan.

12

The fiscal test with development controls

Twelve measures, each tested bivariate and under the strictest specification: log GDP per capita and log population controlled, China and India dropped.

Each row has two dots: the open one is the simple test, the filled one is the strictest. A line running to the left means the evidence got stronger under the controls.

Controls strengthen the tax results, as in the original, but they strengthen nearly everything else too. Under the full gauntlet, non-resource tax gives p = 0.0007, total tax 0.0021 and OWID tax 0.019, all failing bivariate. That part replicates. But rule of law also reaches 0.0004, judicial checks 0.0011, administration 0.010 and corruption 0.017. In the original those four stayed at 0.054–0.68. The result that separated fiscal from institutional capacity does not replicate. Once development is held constant, almost any capacity measure bends.

The finer fiscal claims.
Level vs mixDirect taxes fail (0.28), and indirect taxes pass (0.0016). The original found the opposite. Income taxes fail under the full gauntlet in both (0.26 here, 0.22 originally), though here they pass bivariate (0.017).
Trade-tax relianceIt never produces an inverted U; the quadratic is upright bivariate. Its linear effect survives GDP per capita (p = 0.004) and survives clustering at the firm level (p = 0.0014, down from 10⁻²⁴ naive). The original found it fully explained by GDP.
What remainsThe composite is the steadiest performer across all four specifications (0.0012 / 1.7×10⁻⁶ / 0.0033 / 6.7×10⁻⁷).
13

Is this just rich countries?

Whether plain development, rather than state capacity, is what produces the hump.

Open dot is the measure on its own; filled dot is the same measure with the rival family controlled. Anything left of the dashed line produces a hump.

Here the replication clearly disagrees with the original.
• Development bends on its own: log GDP per capita gives p = 0.0002, HDI 0.034, internet 0.045 and schooling 0.024. Originally all were 0.10–0.45.
• Tax does not survive wealth: non-resource tax with a GDP control gives p = 0.42, against the original's 0.0004.
• The symmetric test (both quadratic, same 158 countries) leaves neither standing: tax 0.57, GDP 0.12. The tax-over-wealth asymmetry is gone.

Two things that do hold.
The composite survives wealthWith log GDP controlled, H-S gives p = 0.0020, and GDP's own coefficient goes insignificant (p = 0.54). The original found this too (0.014, and GDP p = 0.29).
A specification detailNon-resource tax passes with GDP and population controlled (panel 12, p = 0.0012) but fails with GDP alone (0.42). The fiscal result therefore depends on the population control. That is a fragile basis for a mechanism claim.
14

What the inverted U is made of

The inverted U split into the two things that make it: how many firms get created, and what share of them stay independent.

Left and middle are the two ingredients, both of which move in one direction only. Right compares what those two would produce if simply multiplied (dashed) against what actually happens (green).

Both margins replicate; the extra steepness does not. Total creation does not turn over (p = 0.18). The independent share falls monotonically: the linear coefficient is −1.02 with p ≈ 10⁻⁹⁴, and the quadratic bends upward. Multiplying the two fitted margins puts the peak at 1.06 on the raw scale (+0.59 sd), close to the observed 1.18 (+0.72 sd). The original's product peaked at 2.40, far right of where its data turned, which it read as the downturn being "steeper and earlier than the margins can account for". In the replication, the margins account for it: rising creation times falling retention is enough to produce the hump.

The rest holds. The hump is a property of the independent-firm margin only: total 0.18, still-operating 0.099, independent 0.0012. It is not a size effect: independent firms per head still bend (p = 0.024), total firms per head do not (0.74), and India contributes only 5.7% of independent firms. The original's summary sentence stands: above roughly three-quarters of a standard deviation of capacity, firms are absorbed faster than new ones are founded.

15

Which sectors, and where

Every firm sorted into 35 sectors (the 24-sector checklist plus the recurring extras), placed by the average state capacity of its home countries.

Left: where a sector sits on the capacity scale, with dot size showing how many firms it has. Right: what became of its firms. Orange stayed independent, blue was acquired, grey is everything else. Click any row for that sector's full firm list.

Mobility and money still sit lowest, but the spectrum is compressed. The lowest-capacity sectors are ride-hailing (0.51), online pharmacy (0.63), P2P wallets (0.67), ticketing (0.68) and food delivery (0.70). The highest are social and messaging (1.26), car and bike sharing (1.24) and price comparison (1.20). Every sector mean now falls between 0.5 and 1.3, against 0.1–1.7 originally, because the larger sample finds most sectors in most kinds of country.

The main point replicates: sector does not explain the capacity gradient.
Standardising the mixAcquisition by tercile is 7.2 / 15.0 / 29.8% raw and 7.0 / 15.0 / 29.4% with the sector mix held fixed. That retains 99% of the gradient, against the original's 95%.
Inside sectors21 sectors are large enough to compare Low with High, and acquisition is higher in High in all 21. The original could test only 5.
Sector fixed effectsThe clustered capacity coefficient on being acquired goes from +0.813 to +0.839. For staying independent it goes from −0.842 to −0.893.
Asset-lightThe asset-light share is flat across terciles: 82 / 87 / 86%.
16

The same firms, grouped into families

The sectors rolled up into six broad families, ordered by the average state capacity of the countries they appear in.

The bar on the left spans the sectors inside each family, with the dot at the family average. The middle bar is what happened to its firms. On the right, L / M / H is that family's share of the low, medium and high capacity platform economies. Click any row to open the family.

Mobility replicates, finance does not. Mobility and logistics falls from 25.7% of the Low-capacity platform economy to 12.5% of High, close to the original's 22.2→11.8%. Financial services is flat (25.4% to 27.0%), where the original had it falling from 34.4% to 22.1%. Media grows with capacity (5.3→9.8%) and business software too (3.8→7.4%), both as before.

Outcomes by family replicate closely. Financial services (69.8%) and business software (69.5%) stay among the most independent, alongside health, education and work (70.8%). Commerce (27.5% acquired) and media (23.8%) are the most bought, as originally (27.5% and 22.8%). Media again has the lowest independence, 41.6% against 37.7%.

17

Did the American company actually come first?

For every firm whose supposed original has a verifiable founding year (4,261 firms, 89% of the data), the gap between the two. Negative means the "clone" existed before the company it is said to copy.

Each bar is a count of firms at that year-gap. Orange bars to the left of zero are firms that existed before their supposed original; the shaded band is the ±2-year window where neither can be said to have copied the other. On the right, the sectors where the labelling breaks down most often.

About one firm in ten came first, as before.
• Came first: 9.8% predate their analogue (original 12.0%).
• Same year: 3.4% were founded in the same year.
• Close either way: 20.7% sit within two years in either direction (original 23.6%).
• Typical lag: the median firm trails its analogue by 6 years (original 5).

It is still worst where the curve turns. Predating runs 1.1% in Low countries, 7.3% in Medium and 14.7% in High, against 3.1 / 7.2 / 12.4% originally.

The sector detail differs. Real-estate portals are 17.9% backwards, not 45.7%. The worst sectors are now logistics (26.2%), social and messaging (20.0%) and insurtech (18.3%). The same pre-Zillow European portals still appear among the extreme cases: SeLoger (1992) and immowelt (1991). The single largest reversal is GO Inc., the former JapanTaxi, dating to 1977 and coded as an Uber analogue.

Some analogues are not American. 27 named analogues are not US companies, covering 178 firms (4.2% of the firms tested, against the original's 6.6%). Most are Shopify (87 firms) and Spotify (43). The replication analogue lookup marked no strings as placeholders; the original found 51.

18

How fast the copy arrives

Group the firms by when their analogue was founded, and ask how long a domestic equivalent took to appear. The grey line shows the same data grouped the wrong way, which is the trap.

Orange: for platforms founded in each period, the median years until a domestic version appeared. It falls from 12 years to 1. Grey: the same firms grouped by their own founding year instead, which points the other way and means nothing.

This replicates almost exactly. For US platforms founded 1994–99, the median domestic equivalent appeared 12 years later and 12% appeared within two years. For platforms founded 2015–20 the median gap is 1 year, and 60% appear within two years. The original had 11 years and 10% falling to 0 years and 56%. Grouping by the firm's own founding year produces the same spurious rising lag, 2→7 years against the original's 2→9.

The two "patterns that were not real" are only partly dissolved here.
Strong states copy fasterWithin the 2015–19 cohort the Low / Medium / High medians are 8 / 7 / 6 years, nearly flat as in the original. Within 2010–14, though, they are 8 / 4 / 3. The raw gap is mostly age composition, but not entirely.
First movers get boughtWithin the 2010–14 cohort, acquisition runs 29 / 26 / 27 / 20% across lag buckets ≤0, 1–3, 4–7 and ≥8 years. A modest ordering survives where the original found none.

Cells are Lind–Mehlum p-values for an inverted U (smaller means a clearer rise-then-fall). Hover an indicator name for the question V-Dem’s country experts answer. V-Dem v16, 2015 values, standardized; 175 countries alone, 172 with controls.

What the index measures. Whether laws are enforced transparently, independently, predictably and equally, and whether officials themselves obey them. Its 15 inputs fall into five groups: courts (independence of high and lower courts, government compliance with rulings, discipline of judges, bribery in the courts), whether the executive respects the constitution, corruption (bribery and theft by the executive and by ordinary public servants), administration (impartial officials, clear and predictable laws), and access to justice for men and for women. None of them measures taxation or bureaucratic reach.

Creation rises with almost every indicator but does not turn over. A linear rise in all firms created is significant for 13 of 15 indicators. The inverted-U test fails for creation on every indicator except access to justice. Access for women bends marginally on its own (p = 0.048), and both access measures bend once development is controlled (men p = 0.005, women p = 0.0003). So part of the access-to-justice hump in independent firms comes from creation itself turning down, which is not true of the composite.

Still-operating firms mostly just rise. On its own, only access to justice for women bends (p = 0.047). With development controlled, about half the indicators bend weakly, led by access to justice (men 0.003, women 0.0001).

The hump in independent firms comes from a specific subset. Taken alone, the clearest humps are access to justice for women (p = 0.001) and men (0.010), the executive respecting the constitution (0.008) and executive bribery (0.016). Court independence is borderline (0.05–0.07). Compliance with courts, bribery in the courts, bribery and theft by ordinary public servants, impartial administration and predictable laws do not bend. With development controlled almost everything bends, as with every measure on this page, so the bivariate column is the more discriminating one.

The independent share falls with every indicator (all p < 0.001 alone, and all but judicial discipline with controls). As in panel 14, this is the retention margin, and it does not single out any component.

Caution. The 15 indicators correlate 0.56–0.97 with each other and 0.71–0.91 with the composite, so these differences are suggestive, not a decomposition. The pattern that stands out is that the humps come from indicators about whether government obeys the law and people can use the courts against it, not from the quality or honesty of the bureaucracy.

The first six columns are Lind–Mehlum p-values, as in panel 19. The last two are firm-level logit coefficients on being acquired, per standard deviation of the measure, with standard errors clustered by country. “ns” marks p ≥ 0.05. Hover a measure for what it asks.

Narrow property-rights measures do not produce the hump on their own. Taken alone, still-independent firms do not bend on V-Dem property rights for men (p = 0.32), Heritage (0.11) or BTI (0.19). They bend on V-Dem property rights for women (0.019), and clearly on Fraser’s Area 2 (0.005). Fraser’s Area 2 is not a narrow property measure, though: it bundles judicial independence, impartial courts, police reliability and contract enforcement, and it correlates 0.93 with Hanson–Sigman. The sharpest humps are still the executive respecting the constitution (0.008) and access to justice (0.001–0.010).

Property rights do predict acquisition, but no better than the rest. Every measure raises the odds of a firm being acquired. Per standard deviation, the V-Dem property-rights coefficients (0.64, 0.69) are similar to access to justice (0.56, 0.57) and to impartial administration (0.50). With log GDP per capita controlled, V-Dem property rights (0.42, 0.43) and Fraser (0.50) survive; Heritage and BTI do not. Hanson–Sigman beats all of them (0.75 alone, 0.74 with GDP), and it barely moves when GDP is added.

Firm creation and still-operating firms follow the earlier pattern. Nothing bends alone except access to justice for women (p = 0.048). With development controlled, access to justice bends clearly, and property rights for women and Fraser bend more weakly.

Reading. If the mechanism were secure title to assets, the direct property-rights measures should do at least as well as everything else. They do not. What best separates the hump from the monotone measures is whether the executive is itself bound by law and whether citizens can take it to court. Property rights are part of that, but an index that measures the right to own property without measuring constraints on the state picks up less of the pattern. The caveat from panel 19 applies: these measures correlate 0.48–0.93 with each other, so this is a ranking of proxies, not an identified mechanism.

Firm-level logit of being acquired, per standard deviation of the measure, with firm age and sector fixed effects; errors clustered by country. In the “vs” columns the small figure is the rival’s own coefficient in the same model. “ns” marks p ≥ 0.05.

The hump: region fixed effects are the control that separates the measures. With development controlled, dropping China and India, or adding any rival, every measure except BTI keeps its inverted U. Adding region fixed effects removes it for the direct property-rights measures: V-Dem men (p = 0.69), V-Dem women (0.37), Heritage (0.26) and BTI (upright curve). The ones that survive, more weakly, are access to justice for women (0.006), the executive respecting the constitution (0.021), Hanson–Sigman (0.043) and Fraser (0.050). So once you compare countries within the same region, the rise and fall in independent firms tracks constraints on the state, not property rights.

Acquisition: property rights are the most robust predictor. V-Dem property rights for men is the one measure that wins every head-to-head. Against the executive respecting the constitution, access to justice and Hanson–Sigman it stays at +0.34 to +0.38 (p < 0.001), while each rival falls to insignificance in the same model. It also survives region fixed effects, though smaller (+0.23, p = 0.03). Heritage, BTI and the women’s measure lose most head-to-heads. Hanson–Sigman is strongest on its own (+0.51, and +0.64 with region fixed effects) but loses to V-Dem property rights for men when both are in the model.

Reading. The two margins seem to have different drivers. Whether a firm gets bought tracks secure private property, which fits a buyer caring about the title to what it is buying. The shape of the curve, where independent firms peak and then decline, tracks whether the state is bound by law and whether citizens can take it to court. So it is partly about property rights: they explain who gets acquired, but not the hump on their own.

Caveats. Region fixed effects take out a great deal of the cross-country variation these measures rely on, so a null there is weak evidence. Horse races between measures correlated at 0.6–0.8 are fragile: the winner can flip with small changes in sample. Countries with no firms were assigned to regions from the World Bank classification.

The acquisition gradient is not specific to analogues. Per standard deviation of state capacity, the log-odds of being acquired rise by 0.62 for analogues and 0.62 for original startups; the log-odds of still being independent fall by 0.70 for both. The interaction is zero (p = 0.99). Across terciles, original startups go from 90% independent and 3% acquired in low-capacity countries to 54% and 28% in high-capacity ones, close to the analogue pattern. The acquisition result holds with firm age controlled (+0.50), without the 50 firms found through exit or showcase lists (+0.68), and using V-Dem property rights instead of capacity (+0.66).

One thing does differ: who buys. In the same 36 countries, 55% of acquired analogues went to a domestic buyer and 14% to a US buyer. For original startups it is 25% domestic and 53% US. Analogues are mostly consolidated at home; original technology firms are mostly bought from abroad, largely by American companies.

The main weakness: unknown fates. 30% of the original startups have no findable outcome, and these are concentrated in low-capacity countries (47%, against 14% in high). Most are small accelerator-cohort firms whose sites are gone, so many probably closed. Counting them as shut down leaves the acquisition gradient intact (+0.79) but removes the independence gradient (+0.01). For originals, the fall in independence therefore depends on how the unknowns are read; the rise in acquisition does not.

What this sample cannot test. Firms were capped at 15 per country, so the count-based inverted U cannot be checked. It also leans on accelerator and showcase lists, which over-represent survivors in some countries (Japan’s J-Startup list) and exits in others (Israel and South Africa drew partly on exit lists).

23

Creation, acquisition and the hump between them

All firms created, firms acquired (split into domestic and foreign buyers), and firms still independent, across state capacity. The default view averages over the countries near each capacity level, so a stretch of the axis with few countries counts the same as one with many. The right-hand chart shows what share of firms is independent or acquired, and what share of acquisitions go to domestic buyers. In the quadratic view it shows each curve’s growth rate instead.

Firms per country
Composition of firms
All firms created Acquired, all buyers Acquired by a domestic buyer Acquired by a foreign buyer Still independent Countries within ±0.25 (strip under the axis) Venezuela (click for its profile)

Switch views with the buttons above the charts. Hover either chart to read every curve at one capacity level. The grey strip under the left chart shows how many countries each point rests on. Venezuela’s actual counts are marked; click them or its guide line to open its firm list.

What the normalization does. The quadratic curves were already per country, but a quadratic uses one formula for the whole axis. Its shape at the top is therefore set partly by the many countries in the middle, and it has to bend symmetrically. The local average instead takes, at each capacity level, a weighted average of firms per country over the countries nearby (Gaussian weights, bandwidth 0.30). Where few countries sit, the estimate is simply less certain, and the bands widen to show it. Bands are 95% intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of countries.

What changes. Two claims from the quadratic view do not survive:
• Acquisitions do not turn down at the top. Per country they rise to about 17 around capacity 2.2 and stay there within the bands (15.5 at 2.6, 95% interval 9.9–24.6).
• Domestic acquisitions do not collapse. The domestic share of acquisitions is about 41–43% everywhere above capacity 1.7. The quadratic’s fall to 30% at the edge came from the functional form, and so did its significant domestic downturn. Foreign buyers still take the larger share at the top, and their count keeps rising.

What holds. Independent firms still rise and then fall. Per country they peak at about 0.88, with 24.7 firms (interval 17.9–32.2), and fall to 13.7 (9.2–20.3) at the top. Meanwhile creation stays roughly flat at 40–48 firms per country and acquisitions double. The local-average peak sits earlier than the quadratic’s 1.19 because the 0.7–0.9 region holds India and China, the two largest ecosystems.

Per million people (total firms over total population among nearby countries) tells a different story at the top. All five curves keep rising, including independent firms, which roughly level off from capacity 1.7 at about 0.7 per million. This view weights countries by population, so India and China pull the middle of the axis down, and small rich countries dominate the right. The population-offset model reported in panel 14, which gives each country equal weight, still finds a hump (p = 0.024). So whether the independent count falls in absolute terms depends on whether countries or people are the unit.

Shares in the local views are ratios of the smoothed curves. The domestic share is hidden where there is less than about 0.3 acquisition per country, which is too few to split.

What this replication supports. The original's central claim survives a full rebuild on 2.5 times the data. State capacity raises founding and acquisition at once, and the count of independent domestic platforms therefore rises and then falls, peaking about three-quarters of a standard deviation above the mean. The sector, age and population-offset checks all replicate. The fiscal-capacity mechanism does not. The claims that tax, not rule of law, drives the hump, that direct taxes matter and indirect ones do not, and that development cannot produce the hump all reverse or dissolve in the new data. The defensible version is the composite: the Hanson–Sigman index bends, survives wealth, and fits best. Which of its dimensions matters cannot be identified from cross-country variation among such collinear measures.

Limits of the replication.
• Same kind of research: the data were again gathered by AI agents from web sources. The replication tests whether an independent re-collection agrees, not whether either collection is complete.
• No facts from memory remain: every value that rested on an agent’s own knowledge was either sourced, corrected or blanked. Blanking raised the number of firms without a founding year from 429 to 507.
• Unknown outcomes: 204 firms still have no known outcome. The headline test does not depend on how they are coded.
• Searches cut short: the web-search allowance ran low partway through. Later agents relied on news-site search APIs, app stores and company pages, and some small countries were searched thinly.
• Newer data releases: covariate vintages differ from the original's: GRD 2025 against 2022, and V-Dem v16.
